newsitem.title: UK: LME seeks sensible balance on changes - CEO.
newsitem.headline: LME seeks sensible balance on changes - CEO.

text.p: Evolution at the London Metal Exchange (LME) as it implements changes prompted by 1996's Sumitomo Corp crisis has to be handled sensibly, in order not to drive business away, Chief Executive David King said.
The LME has already amended its constitution to re-structure its Board and will report more frequently on inventory movements from next month.
It is now tackling the issue of greater transparency on large positions and warehouse holdings of metal and studying systems used in other countries, but in a way that would not deter business.
"The last thing the market needs is for liquidity to be driven away...we have to find a sensible balance," King said in a telephone interview.
So far the LME has not made any final decisions, but the sub-committees charged with implementing changes are in constant discussion with market members and users.
As part of this process, the LME has seriously looked at the U.S. CFTC (Commodity Futures Trading Commission) Commitments of Traders Report.
"This is a mechanism that we could adapt and modify to suit our needs," King said.
The LME version would possibly entail declaring that particular participants held long or short positions of a certain size without naming the companies concerned.
And unlike the CFTC report, the LME would not specify whether the positions were commercial or non-commercial - essentialy trade or speculative.
On warehouse stocks, the LME might report in a similar fashion that one company held a certain percentage of the inventory, again without divulging the name of the firm.
"It puts information into the public domain, but it does not frighten market participants," King said.
However, there are practical difficulties in defining stock-ownership, for example.
"If a holder has pledged metal to a bank then who is the legitimate owner of the warrants? LME warrants are bearer bonds, so it is not easy to say who owns them," he said.
"It is not any easy thing to achieve, but we are seeking to address that difficulty."
Regarding price transparency, the Exchange is proposing to enhance current information and add further data, incorporating highs, lows, volumes, values and open interest on futures and options.
Consequently, the LME has retained technology consultants to develop systems to make this infomation available via vendor feeds, King added.
The whole raft of reforms the LME is making followed last December's review by U.K.regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) of the market prompted by the Sumitomo copper affair.

Last June, the Japanese company announced losses that eventually totalled $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised copper trades allegedly carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka, who is now being charged with fraud and forgery.
